faq.a: Adult worms lack the glutamate‑gated chloride channels that ivermectin targets, so the drug only kills microfilariae and larvae.
faq.q: Why does ivermectin spare adult filarial worms?

faq.a: No; diethylcarbamazine or albendazole are preferred because ivermectin does not affect Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae sufficiently.
faq.q: Can ivermectin be used for lymphatic filariasis?

faq.a: High microfilarial loads can trigger a severe encephalopathic reaction after ivermectin.

exam: A patient from a river‑valley presents with pruritic papules and visual disturbances – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a skin snip; a positive microfilariae count confirms onchocerciasis and guides MDA.

In a HIV‑positive man with chronic diarrhoea and eosinophilia, stool microscopy is negative – how would you confirm strongyloidiasis? — Use Baermann concentration or serology; a negative result does not exclude hyperinfection, so treat empirically if suspicion high.
Why is ivermectin contraindicated in a traveller with high Loa loa microfilaraemia? — High microfilarial load can cause fatal encephalopathy after drug‑induced rapid killing.
A child with crusted scabies is not responding to topical permethrin – what systemic therapy is indicated? — Give oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg; it reaches skin layers where mites reside.

During a community MDA for onchocerciasis, a pregnant woman refuses treatment – how do you counsel her? — Explain that ivermectin is contraindicated in pregnancy; schedule treatment postpartum and emphasize vector control.

A patient on steroids develops severe respiratory distress after a week of diarrhoea – what parasitic complication should you suspect? — Strongyloides hyperinfection; start ivermectin promptly and discontinue steroids if possible.
What is the rationale for combining albendazole with ivermectin in mass treatment programmes? — Albendazole adds activity against soil‑transmitted helminths, broadening community protection.
How does ivermectin’s mechanism differ from that of benzimidazoles? — Ivermectin opens chloride channels causing paralysis; benzimidazoles inhibit tubulin polymerisation, affecting worm metabolism.
ai.title: Ivermectin in Tropical Parasitic Diseases
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Ivermectin is a broad‑spectrum antiparasitic used mainly for onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis and scabies. It kills microfilariae and larval stages by enhancing glutamate‑gated chloride channels, sparing adult worms in many infections.

b: Effective against microfilariae, larvae of Strongyloides, Onchocerca, and ectoparasites
Not active against adult filarial worms
sections.p: Ivermectin is a macrocyclic lactone derived from Streptomyces avermitilis. It is lipophilic, concentrates in skin and adipose tissue, and is excreted mainly in feces.

b: Onchocerca volvulus – skin‑dwelling microfilariae cause river blindness
Strongyloides stercoralis – autoinfection cycle can lead to hyperinfection
Sarcoptes scabiei – burrows in epidermis, causing intense pruritus
sections.p: Target parasites share glutamate‑gated chloride channels absent in mammals, allowing selective paralysis.

b: Larvae develop in the skin, then migrate to lungs or circulate as microfilariae
Autoinfection allows chronic infection without re‑exposure
sections.p: Onchocerciasis is transmitted by black‑fly bites; Strongyloides penetrates skin from contaminated soil; scabies spreads by prolonged skin‑to‑skin contact.

b: Onchocerciasis: pruritic papules, skin depigmentation, ocular lesions → blindness
Strongyloidiasis: abdominal pain, diarrhoea, eosinophilia; hyperinfection → sepsis, respiratory failure
Scabies: intense nocturnal itch, burrows, secondary bacterial infection
sections.p: Clinical manifestations depend on parasite load and immune response.
Laboratory confirmation is often limited in low‑resource settings; clinical picture guides therapy.

t.b: Detects Onchocerca microfilariae; positive confirms river blindness

t.a: Stool agar plate or Baermann technique
t.b: Detects Strongyloides larvae; positive supports strongyloidiasis
Shows scabies mites or eggs; if unavailable, treat empirically based on classic burrows

b: Onchocerciasis: 150 µg/kg once yearly; reduces transmission, not adult worms
Strongyloidiasis: 200 µg/kg daily for 2 days; repeat in immunocompromised patients
Scabies: 200 µg/kg single dose; repeat in 1‑2 weeks if crusted
sections.p: Ivermectin is given as a single oral dose (or repeated for strongyloidiasis) because it rapidly reduces microfilarial load.

t.b: DEC for lymphatic filariasis; albendazole for soil‑transmitted helminths; avoid ivermectin in high‑load Loa loa due to encephalopathy
Annual ivermectin + albendazole for onchocerciasis control; community compliance essential

b: Never give ivermectin to a patient with high Loa loa microfilaraemia (>30 000 mf/mL) – risk of fatal encephalopathy
In strongyloidiasis, look for eosinophilia >500 cells/µL and consider HIV or steroids as risk factors for hyperinfection
Onchocerciasis ocular involvement is a public‑health indication for community MDA
sections.p: Focus on differentiating when ivermectin is indicated versus contraindicated, and on recognizing hyperinfection syndromes.

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock or respiratory failure in strongyloidiasis hyperinfection
Severe secondary bacterial infection of scabies lesions
